skyline.text: Why we fail to communicate, from Amit Varma’s writing course
A hundred thousand see your title; a hundred finish the paper
Printing was once the limit; now it is winning attention

brief.head: Ten thousand universes
brief.text: Economics has outgrown its “physics illusion”, Ajay Shah said. With about 10,000 important datasets, each its own little universe, it now solves one puzzle at a time. {#datasets}

brief.head: Diabetes, by country
brief.text: Even medicine can turn local, Shah said: if Indian DNA matters, diabetes in India may differ from diabetes in China. Physics, by contrast, is universal. {062-C03}

brief.head: Marx’s epitaph
brief.text: Some research seeks only to understand the world, Shah said; some aims to act in it, in the spirit of Karl Marx’s epitaph: “the point, however, is to change it.” {062-J14}

brief.head: A bonfire of journals
brief.text: Amit Varma proposed a party: get every academic they know completely drunk, gather a bunch of journals, and hold “a bonfire of the journals”. {062-J05}

brief.head: Who gets the byline
brief.text: Authors invent and assistants implement, Ajay Shah said. Assistants are thanked on the front page; only original creative work earns authorship. {#authors}

thought.text: Importance is in the eye of the beholder.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, refusing the gatekeepers’ claim to know which research questions matter

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah gives a masterclass on research writing
lead.head: Gentle readers, gentle writers
body: Ajay Shah promised at the outset that by the end of his masterclass on how to write a paper, “our gentle readers will become gentle writers”. {062-J01}

Amit Varma made clear the hour was not only for academics. Think of a paper, he said, as a proxy for any attempt at a novel insight: how to organise knowledge, what rigour it needs, how to craft and structure it.
The structure of what you write, Varma argued, shapes the structure of how you think. So this was also meant as a masterclass on how to think.
Shah defined the word just as broadly. A paper, for him, is a unit of knowledge: a newspaper article, a blog post, a working paper or a journal article. New insight is what counts.
## The machine and its gatekeepers

Varma began with Larry White’s picture of an idea pipeline, from lonely researchers to commentators to the public, and asked whether it still works. In an earlier episode, the hosts had argued that much of academia has become a circle game.
Shah was frank about journals. They once spread knowledge; now they hand out credentials.
“Journal publication is there for the sole purpose of credentials,” he said. “I got a pub in this journal, please give me a job, please give me a grant.” {062-C04}
A good paper, he said, needs a clear question, a persuasive answer and novelty. {062-C05}
Which questions count as important is another matter, and Shah rejected the gatekeepers’ snobbery. Varma went further: peer review, he said, makes him want to puke.
## Writing for the reader
Varma brought in the lesson of his writing course. Communication has two variables, you and your reader, and most writers ignore the second.

Shah agreed. Writing a research paper, he said, “is a lot more like writing than researchers care to admit”. Readers do not want the researcher’s life story, only the question, the approach and the findings.
He offered structures to start from: IMRD for science papers, and an economics recipe that opens with a 1,000-word summary disguised as an introduction.
His rule of thumb for readership is sobering. About 100,000 people see a paper’s title, 10,000 read the abstract, 1,000 start the paper and 100 finish it. {062-C12}

So he writes inside out: the body first, then the conclusions, the introduction and the abstract, and the title last. His teams first build each paper as a dense internal slideshow, refined meeting by meeting until it stops changing.
## After the last full stop
A finished paper still has to be pushed, through blog posts, newspaper pieces, videos and talks. Shah prefers small rooms, where ten focused people can be persuaded, to big conferences.
He does not think the world picked his best papers, and he is at peace with that.
None of it comes quickly. A sad fact of the modern world, Shah said, is that “most people who have finished a PhD are actually quite bad at writing papers”. {062-C16}
His recommendations were for the craft itself: the simple Strunk and White, and Varma’s *Art of Clear Writing* course.
Varma had a grievance of a different kind. Authors are often listed alphabetically, and his surname begins with V. “There’s no great economist called Zimbalist,” he said.

second.label: Global journals
second.head: Open the windows at home
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why global journals publish SEC trivia but ignore SEBI
body: For Indian social scientists, Ajay Shah said, the nightmare from global journals is a familiar verdict: “this is not an interesting question.” {062-S02}

Any obscure regulation change at the United States SEC, he said, is worthy of the top finance journals. The drama of regulatory changes by SEBI, “arguably the world’s most activist financial regulator”, is dismissed: it’s India. So researchers contort their work to shed light on “the grand questions of the age as seen in Germany”.

Shah would rather they looked at the reality around them. That, he said, “creates the energy and the emotional resilience to chase those questions”, and to deliver their jewels to the world. {#resilience}

quote.text: I think that we should open the windows of our house and look out at the reality

second.caption: global journals and SEBI

third.head: Best work, least cited
body: Amit Varma asked how a creator copes when work is ignored. His own habit, he said, is to finish an episode with full intensity, then forget it and move on.

Ajay Shah pointed to his page on Google Scholar, where some papers were cited and many were not. “When I look at the list, I don’t agree,” he said. “I don’t think that the world chose my good stuff.” {062-S08}
He is at peace with it. The archive exists, and somebody may come to it a hundred years from now. {#archive}

His enthusiasm for any paper suffers “some exponential decay”, he said, so he talks only about work that still excites him: right now, his innovation-policy paper with R.A. Mashelkar and Susan Thomas. His rule for talks is simple. “Never do a boring talk.” {#dulltalk}
third.caption: the papers the world passed over

p2.title: The paper chase
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s masterclass, chapter by chapter, from how the research machine works to why the craft takes years

sections.label: The machine
sections.head: Credentials, not circulation
sections.caption: the sociology of research
body: Amit Varma opened with a passage from Larry White’s *The Clash of Economic Ideas*, which he called a fantastic book. Ideas, it suggests, travel like timber: abstract researchers produce them, applied researchers turn them into policy ideas, and journalists and intellectuals carry them to the public. {062-C01}
Ajay Shah said the landscape has changed. He described a “physics illusion” in the social sciences, the hope of single grand theories that apply everywhere.

Instead, economics has become a set of subcultures, each working on one dataset. The 20 people who know the CMIE household survey, he said, share code and concepts, read each other’s papers and cite each other. {#cmie}
“It’s better to be loyal to the reality rather than settle for a sweet abstraction,” Shah said. {062-C02}
## A paper, not a pub

For the episode, Shah set aside the journal article as the meaning of “paper”. A paper is any building block of new knowledge, and knowledge is a graph of such papers, used by individuals, firms and governments.
Journals, he said, now serve only as credentials. A mature reader can judge a paper directly: does it give me a new idea, does it make me change my mind? {062-C04}

~ Knowing the sociology of how this machine works, Shah said, helps a reader “shrug off some of the showboating” that authors do to get published. {062-J13} Varma declared it the phrase that embodies the show.

quote.text: Today the dissemination function is 100% gone. You never need to go to the journal website to get the paper.

sections.label: The three tests
sections.head: Is it new? Is it true?
sections.caption: the three tests of a paper
body: Every paper in science or social science, Ajay Shah said, needs three things: clarity on a question, an answer that persuades rather than making “some random claims”, and novelty. {062-C05}
A summary of the state of the art is useful, he said, but it is not a paper. “You could expect a LLM to read 20 papers and summarise them.” {#llm}
The same tests make a good referee report. Shah would ask a reviewer to write down the paper’s question and its answer afresh. In a confused paper, neither can be readily culled out.
## Whose question matters?

Then there is importance. Global warming is probably important, Shah said, and the headgear of some tribals in Chandrapur district probably is not. But “importance is in the eye of the beholder”. {062-C06}

Amit Varma raised “the radical possibility that the headgear of the Chandrapur tribals causes global warming”. Shah, straight-faced, wondered about obscure chemicals in the headgear triggering reactions in the upper atmosphere. {062-J03}

~ Researchers do not waste their time, Shah argued. If someone has put real effort into a question, others should assume it matters to someone, as the establishment failed to see with every maverick. {#time}

quote.text: What’s the question? Is the clarity on the question? What’s the answer? Is the answer persuasive? And a test. Is it novel?

sections.label: The reader first
sections.head: It takes two to write
sections.caption: putting the reader first
body: Amit Varma put to Ajay Shah the question he asks in the first webinar of his writing course. We learn many difficult things easily, so why do we fail at communicating, even with friends in a cafe or with a loved one?
Shah’s answer pointed to Broca’s area, the part of the brain that does speech. Varma called it “a deeply technical answer” that was “absolutely correct”. {062-J06}
His own answer: learning has one variable, yourself, while communicating has two. Writing, he said, only becomes meaningful when it has the intended effect on the intended reader. {062-C08}
## The life story can wait
Shah agreed, and turned on his own profession. Researchers cut corners on writing, he said, and that is wrong: the purpose of a paper is to change the mind of a cynical reader. {062-C09}
Research is a mountain climb of fumbles, dead ends and aha moments, but the paper should leave the climb out. “They don’t want to know your life story,” Shah said of readers. {062-C10}
~ The journey can also change the destination, he added: set out for India and you may find the route to America. {#india} Then you write about the route to America.

quote.text: Communicating is tough because there are two variables.

sections.label: The skeleton
sections.head: Structure before swagger
sections.caption: the structure of a paper
body: Beginners, Ajay Shah said, should stick to standard structures. Once they find their powers, they can smash the boundaries. {062-C11}

In science, the default is IMRD. {#imrd} The introduction summarises what is known and ends with the questions. Methods must be detailed enough for third parties to replicate the work. Results report what was found without much interpretation; discussion asks what it means and where research should go next.

Shah called it “a low bullshit way to do scientific communication”. He had also cited the Leap Blog without explaining it, and Amit Varma caught him: “You just committed the curse of knowledge.” {062-J07}
## The economist’s recipe

For economics, Shah uses a title, a 100-word abstract, and an introduction that is really a 1,000-word executive summary, often published separately in a newspaper or on a blog. Then come the setting and questions, methods and results, robustness checks against alternative explanations, and a conclusion that asks: so what?
Most care goes to the top. “A hundred thousand people are going to read the title of your paper, so make it count,” Shah said. {062-C12}
~ Brevity is work too. Varma quoted Blaise Pascal, who ended a long letter to a friend: “I’m sorry this letter is so long, I did not have time to make it short.” {062-J18}

quote.text: as you grow up, you find your powers, then you can smash the boundaries and do things in novel ways

sections.label: The act of writing
sections.head: Inside out, title last
sections.caption: writing inside out
body: Writing changes your mind as you go, Ajay Shah said, so the tidy plan of title first, then abstract, then paper rarely works. Amit Varma reached for Joan Didion: “I write to find out what I think.” {062-J19}
Shah writes inside out: the body of the paper first, then the conclusions. “Then write the introduction. Then write the abstract and last write the title.” {#insideout}

Writing is costly, he said, but don’t love text just because you produced it. When a chunk is weak he deletes it and starts again, “because I find the mind is cleaner when writing from scratch”. {062-C13}
## A slideshow nobody sees
His teams build each paper first as an internal slideshow of 40 to 50 slides, with every table, graph and citation in the order of the argument. Every meeting turns up errors and new ideas.

The assistants, who are apprentices, implement them. Each time, Shah said, they must come back “with an absolutely perfect product in the opinion of the apprentice”. {#apprentice} When the meetings stop producing changes, the search has converged, and the slides become prose.

~ Varma set this apart from Jeff Bezos’s rule at Amazon, “do not bring me an effing powerpoint”: a presentation simplifies, while this deck holds everything. Shah agreed that it is only an internal technique to reach the paper. {062-C14}

quote.text: So we should never take this slideshow and try to take it to an audience. This is just a development platform.

sections.label: Lessons learnt
sections.head: The long apprenticeship
sections.caption: a lifetime of learning the craft
body: Asked what years of writing papers had taught him, Ajay Shah began with a confession: when he was young, he grossly underestimated how hard it would be. {062-S07}
He read papers early and assumed he would slide from reading them to writing them. He was wrong. Writing papers, he said, is a craft, and like every craft it takes practice.

He has learnt in two ways. He looks back dispassionately at what he did a year or two ago, and he studies papers that leave him “shocked at how perfect and how well done this is”, asking how the authors did it. {#shocked}
## Life after the PhD

A PhD does not finish the training, Shah said. Fresh PhDs often feel ready to go and write papers; unfortunately, he said, that is not true. It takes many years after the PhD to imagine a research project and get it done in a leadership role. {062-C16}
“It’s a very long childhood, it’s a long apprenticeship where people learn,” he said. {#childhood}
~ His advice to everyone was to approach the work “with a suitable level of respect that you’re going to climb a mountain”. {#mountain}

quote.text: When I was young, I was a little too optimistic that it will be easy, I’ll transition from reading papers to writing papers.

side.boxText: Researchers, Ajay Shah said, grossly underestimate the craft of writing, absorbed as they are in econometrics or computer science. His prescription: make the simple Strunk and White universal knowledge, and attend Amit Varma’s *Art of Clear Writing* class. {062-R13}

contQuote.text: Think of the reader. I wish to say something to the reader. I wish to change the mind of the reader, which is very hard.

p3.title: Tales from the paper trail
p3.deck: Four stories from Ajay Shah’s decades of writing papers, and what they teach

stories.start: I guess the good titles matter. Uh titles should not just be cute
stories.end: there are titles that are almost disconnected with the main body of the work
stories.caption: cute titles and good ones
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a title that kept luring him back
stories.head: The title that cried wolf
body: There is one paper Ajay Shah will not name, and he will not name its authors either. But its title, he said, is very cute, and he has thought about it for years.
The title dragged him back to read the paper several times. Each time, the paper was not about the title. {062-S04}

“Titles should not just be cute, they should also be about the paper,” Shah said. A title is a one-sentence summary, and a literary flourish helps. But the urge for cuteness, he thinks, is a bit overdone.

Amit Varma offered one that gets it right. In the early 1990s, as Varma recalled, Vijayendra Rao studied dowry and how it was changing, and called his paper *The Rising Price of Husbands*. “It’s clever and it is about the paper,” Varma said. {062-R07}

Shah offered one of his own, written with colleagues including Ayush Patnaik and Susan Thomas: *But Clouds Got in My Way*. “What a great title,” said Varma. It is about clouds, Shah explained: clouds interfering with infrared radiation going up to a satellite.
Varma later pictured the end of that laborious paper: the authors sitting back, putting on some Joni Mitchell, and finding the line in “the great song”, *Both Sides Now*. {062-R09}
~ The stakes are high, Shah said, because the title is what most readers will ever see. Of 100,000 who see it, about 100 will finish the paper.
stories.why: A title is the one sentence most readers will ever see. Wit can earn their attention, but a title that is not about the paper wastes it, and the author’s credibility too. The best, like Rao’s, are clever and accurate at once.

stories.start: In history, Uh what people did was that they would write a letter
stories.end: the number of pages per issue of a journal. All these concepts are obsolete.
stories.caption: the Royal Society’s letters
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how journals began, and what they are for now
stories.head: From letters to letterheads
body: Research communication, Ajay Shah said, began with a letter. A scientist would write to the Secretary of the Royal Society in London to say: I did this new work. {062-S01}
The Secretary gathered these letters into a publication that went out to all the members. Out of those beginnings grew modern journals, and their job was dissemination.

That job, Shah said, is now “100% gone”. Mature working papers, blog articles and newspaper articles carry important new knowledge, and nobody needs a journal website to get a paper. Journals survive as brand names that help you get a job or a grant. {062-C04}
~ The world, he said, is back to the Royal Society’s unstructured, everyone-to-everyone model. Amit Varma noted one difference: today there is no Royal Society in between.
stories.why: Institutions can outlive their purpose and become credential machines. Once you see that journals certify careers rather than spread knowledge, Shah argued, you can judge a paper on its merits, not on where it appeared.

stories.start: we talked about Mendel, and I had a fun fact, a trivia
stories.end: but nobody in this world bothered to read that paper.
stories.caption: Mendel’s forty copies
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the work that starts when writing ends
stories.head: The flood after the press
body: In *The Outlaws*, an earlier episode, Ajay Shah recalled, he had shared a piece of trivia: Mendel ordered forty copies of his paper from the press. {062-S03}
Today there is no such limit. “At the same time, the world is deluged with too much rubbish,” Shah said. Put a finished paper on a website and the world is not waiting to read it.

So the work continues after the writing: newspaper pieces, blog posts, a video, talks. Small rooms matter, he said, because when you are put into a room with two hundred people and given ten minutes, nothing gets done. {#room200}

~ Skip it, he warned, and a hundred years from now famous YouTubers will make a show about your paper on the website of IIM Kozhikode, “but nobody in this world bothered to read that paper”. {062-J10}

quote.text: it’s a stone that will just skip over the lake and it’ll be gone

stories.start: And your your most frequent co-author is Susan Thomas.
stories.end: the game or different communities operate different rules of the
stories.caption: why it’s Shah and Thomas
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the order of names on a paper
stories.head: S before T, nothing more
body: Amit Varma pointed out that Ajay Shah’s most frequent co-author is Susan Thomas. When people see a Shah and Thomas paper, Shah said, they assume it is because he is “the cool guy”. {062-S05}
In fact the names are alphabetical. Her work or role, he said, is in no way inferior to his: S simply comes before T.

Shah likes the convention because it leaves only one fight, over whether you get authorship at all. Once you do, everyone is equal. Otherwise, he said, the possible orderings multiply to n-factorial, and there is fight upon fight.

~ Varma, whose surname starts with V, recalled research from Malcolm Gladwell’s *Outliers*: top athletes tend to be born early in the year, because age-group cut-offs fall on 1 January. {#january} He was born in December. “I had no chance.” {062-J12}
stories.why: A good convention removes a fight that would otherwise happen. It also means readers should not read hierarchy into author order without knowing the rules of the field. Different communities, Shah said, play by different rules.

quiz.q: What three things, according to Ajay Shah, does every paper in science or social science need?
quiz.a: A clearly stated question, a persuasive answer, and novelty in the work.

quiz.q: What do the letters IMRD stand for in the standard structure of a science paper?
quiz.a: Introduction, methods, results and discussion: the default skeleton of a STEM paper.

quiz.q: Why does Shah often delete a weak chunk of a paper rather than edit it?
quiz.a: He finds the mind is cleaner writing from scratch than tinkering with old stuff.

quiz.q: Which song did Amit Varma imagine giving *But Clouds Got in My Way* its title?
quiz.a: Joni Mitchell’s *Both Sides Now*, which Varma called “the great song”.

quiz.q: Why does Shah prefer a room of ten people to a room of two hundred?
quiz.a: Thirty to fifty minutes with ten focused people actually changes minds.

quiz.q: What, according to Amit Varma, makes communicating harder than learning difficult things?
quiz.a: Learning involves one variable, yourself; communicating involves two, you and the other person.
